analysis.one_liner: Makes gasoline and fuel price gouging a federal offense with FTC enforcement and stiff penalties.
analysis.headline: The price gouging bill never left committee: it was referred to a House committee and a subcommittee and died there without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make it an unfair or deceptive practice under the Federal Trade Commission Act to sell crude oil, gasoline, diesel, home heating oil, or biofuel at a price the FTC defines as price gouging [S2] [S3]. The FTC would have to write rules defining price gouging within six months, and enforcement would go to the FTC, the Attorney General, and state attorneys general, with civil penalties up to triple the overcharge plus daily fines and criminal fines up to $150 million for wholesale violations [S2] [S3]. The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its consumer protection subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Drivers, households that heat with oil, and anyone who buys gasoline or diesel. Consumers overcharged during price spikes could be made whole through civil penalties, with the recovered overcharges deposited into state consumer compensation funds or state general funds [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Drivers and home heating oil customers

how_it_helps.text: Makes selling crude oil, gasoline, diesel fuel, home heating oil, or biofuel at a price that constitutes price gouging an unfair or deceptive practice under the FTC Act, a first federal floor against fuel price gouging.
Requires the FTC to define 'price gouging' by rule within six months of enactment, closing the gap that let sellers charge whatever supply disruptions would bear.

Sets civil penalties at triple the overcharge, plus up to $3 million per day for continuing wholesale violations, and criminal fines of up to $150 million and two years' imprisonment for wholesale violations.
Lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents, and requires that the recovered overcharge portion of penalties be deposited into state consumer compensation funds or state general funds.

analysis.who_pays: Oil refiners, wholesalers, and fuel retailers who price above fair market levels; the heaviest penalties fall on wholesale sellers, who face treble damages, daily fines, and criminal exposure. Some compliance and litigation costs would likely be passed into fuel prices for compliant sellers as well.

drawbacks.text: The bill never defines price gouging itself; it leaves the definition to FTC rules, so sellers would face treble damages and criminal exposure under a standard written after the fact by regulators, which could chill normal pricing during volatile markets.

Enforcement is exclusive to the FTC, the U.S. Attorney General, and state attorneys general, and state actions are barred while a federal action is pending, replacing state-level fuel gouging laws with a single federal standard that may be narrower in practice.

Penalties aimed at price spikes could discourage supply when it is scarcest, if sellers hold fuel off the market rather than risk pricing above a federal fair-market standard — a cost that lands on the same consumers the bill protects.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For consumers hit by fuel price spikes, the bill offered real money: treble-damage penalties, daily fines, and recovered overcharges routed to state consumer funds. Its weakness is design, not intent: the key term, price gouging, would be defined only later by FTC rule, creating uncertainty for sellers and enforcement risk that a fair-market benchmark could misfire during genuinely scarce markets. On balance the consumer benefit is substantial and the main costs are borne by sellers charging above-market prices, with a real risk of side effects on supply incentives.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its subcommittee from the day it was introduced until the Congress ended, and no vote ever happened.

narrative.text: Rep. Heather Wilson introduced the bill on May 15, 2007.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce and then to the Subcommittee on Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection.
No further action — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — is recorded for the rest of the 110th Congress, which ended January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Fuel sellers are better off: no federal price gouging prohibition or penalties were ever created, and the FTC and state attorneys general never gained the enforcement tools the bill would have given them.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and fuel sellers, largely untouched

for.name: Rep. Heather Wilson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to prohibit fuel price gouging.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. John Dingell (D-MI)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup, letting it die in committee for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Petroleum and fuel marketing industries
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal price gouging penalties, which would impose treble damages, daily fines, and criminal exposure on fuel sellers.

sides.party_line_note: The bill was a Republican effort — a Republican sponsor and 8 Republican cosponsors — while the Democratic-majority committee that controlled its fate took no action on it, so its death reflects committee inaction across parties rather than a party-line vote.

industries.industry: Oil refiners and crude oil sellers
industries.note: Would face treble-damage civil penalties, fines up to $3 million per day for continuing wholesale violations, and criminal fines up to $150 million for pricing above a federally defined fair market level. Their gain is the public's cost when prices spike.

industries.industry: Gasoline, diesel, and heating oil retailers and wholesalers
industries.note: The bill makes retail and wholesale fuel price gouging a federal offense punishable by treble overcharges, fines up to $2 million, and two years' imprisonment. Higher litigation and compliance costs could partly flow into fuel prices for all buyers.
Biofuels are covered by the same price gouging prohibition as fossil fuels, but inclusion treats renewable fuel sellers as part of a consumer-protected fuel market rather than a favored carve-out.
